title: Autoscaling
subtitle: Watch a lunchtime traffic spike hit a fleet, and see why reacting late hurts and how schedules and forecasts help.
learn: How reactive, scheduled, and predictive scaling differ and when each fits
Which metrics make good scaling signals (and which mislead)
Why scaling lag exists: metric delay + boot time + warm-up
How cooldowns stop the fleet from flapping up and down
The cost of over-provisioning versus the risk of under-provisioning

steps.title: How many servers do you need?
steps.body: An online shop gets 600 requests per second most of the day. Assume one instance (one server) comfortably handles 100 requests per second at 60 percent CPU, so 6 instances is the right size. But the number you need changes through the day, and nobody wants to watch a dashboard and add servers by hand. Autoscaling is software that changes the instance count for you.
steps.idea: The right fleet size moves with traffic; autoscaling is the control loop that follows it.
steps.caption: Steady state: 6 instances at 60% CPU.

steps.title: The lunch spike arrives
steps.body: At 11:45 a promotion email goes out and traffic doubles to 1,200 requests per second within a minute. Six instances are now facing twice the load. At 60 percent CPU they handled 600, so at 100 percent their ceiling is only about 1,000. CPU maxes out and requests queue up. p95 latency (the time within which 95 percent of requests finish) jumps from 120 ms to about 1.8 seconds, and some requests time out.
steps.idea: Too little capacity does not degrade gently: queues build up and latency explodes.
steps.caption: Demand doubles, but capacity does not.

steps.title: Pick a signal to scale on
steps.body: Every instance reports numbers to a metrics store, usually averaged per minute. Here they report CPU at 100 percent. Good signals rise with load and move before users suffer: average CPU, requests per instance, or for queue workers the queue length or the age of the oldest message. Memory is often a poor signal, because many runtimes keep their memory after a spike. Latency is a useful alarm, but it rises only after users are already hurting.
steps.idea: Scale on a metric that rises with load and falls when capacity is added, ideally one that moves early.
steps.caption: Instances publish their CPU to the metrics store.

steps.title: Reactive: react to what happened
steps.body: A reactive policy compares a metric with a target. With target tracking you say "keep average CPU near 60 percent". The autoscaler computes desired = current x (measured / target): 6 x 100 / 60 = 10, so it asks the cloud API for 4 more instances. The catch: CPU cannot go above 100 percent, so a saturated fleet hides how overloaded it really is. Unsaturated, the load would read 120 percent, and 6 x 120 / 60 = 12. The real need was 12.
steps.idea: Reactive scaling is simple and handles surprises, but it only acts after the load has already arrived.
steps.caption: The autoscaler decides on +4 and calls the cloud API.

steps.title: Scaling lag
steps.body: Help is not instant. Metrics are averaged per minute, so the spike is noticed about a minute late. The scaler may wait for a couple of readings to avoid false alarms. Then the cloud must start a virtual machine and boot your app, often 60 to 120 seconds. All that time users still see 1.8 s latency. Typically 3 to 5 minutes pass between the spike and relief.
steps.idea: Scaling lag is metric delay plus decision delay plus boot time plus warm-up, and reactive scaling always pays it.
steps.caption: New instances are booting; none are serving traffic yet.

steps.title: Warm-up and the second round
steps.body: The 4 new instances join, and the load balancer sends them traffic. They start cold: empty caches, no open database connections yet, code not yet optimized by the runtime. So for a minute or so they run below full speed. With 10 instances sharing 1,200 req/s (120 each), CPU settles around 72 percent, still above the 60 percent target, so the scaler adds 2 more (10 x 72 / 60 = 12). Once warm, 12 instances run at 60 percent and p95 returns to about 130 ms.
steps.idea: A new instance is not at full capacity the moment it boots, so give it a warm-up period before trusting its metrics.
steps.caption: The fleet grows from 6 to 10 to 12 and latency recovers.

steps.title: Scaling in, slowly
steps.body: At 12:30 the spike ends and traffic falls back to 600 req/s, so CPU drops to 30 percent on 12 instances. The scaler does not remove half the fleet at once. A cooldown (say 5 to 10 minutes) and removing only a few instances at a time make scale-in slower than scale-out. Without that, a short dip would remove servers just before the next wave, and the fleet would flap up and down, paying boot lag every time.
steps.idea: Scale out fast and scale in slowly: removing capacity too early costs more than keeping it a bit longer.
steps.caption: Traffic falls, so instances are removed a few at a time, back toward 6.

steps.title: Scheduled: you know the pattern
steps.body: The spike happens every weekday at 11:45, so waiting for CPU to rise is wasteful. A scheduled action raises the minimum to 12 instances at 11:35, leaving time to boot and warm up, and a second action lowers it back to 6 after the peak. The spike now meets full capacity with no lag. The cost is a few extra instance-hours, and the schedule goes stale if the pattern changes, such as on a holiday or when marketing changes the send time.
steps.idea: Scheduled scaling removes lag for predictable load, but it is only as good as your calendar.
steps.caption: Capacity is added before the spike arrives.

steps.title: Predictive: let history forecast
steps.body: Predictive scaling learns from past load, typically days to a couple of weeks of history, to forecast the next day or so and launch capacity early. It suits regular daily and weekly patterns without hand-written schedules. It cannot see a surprise, like a viral post. So teams combine all three: a forecast or schedule for the known shape, reactive scaling as a safety net, and sensible minimum and maximum limits.
steps.idea: Forecasts handle regular rhythms; reactive scaling covers what the forecast cannot know.
steps.caption: A forecast feeds the autoscaler ahead of time, while live CPU keeps watch.

steps.title: Choosing a policy
steps.body: Reactive scaling follows live metrics and handles surprises but lags 3 to 5 minutes. Scheduled scaling removes lag for known events. Predictive scaling learns the rhythm. Set a minimum so you survive the first seconds of a spike, a maximum so a bug cannot buy 500 servers, and headroom (a 60 percent target, not 90) because capacity arrives late. Idle headroom is cheap: 6 extra instances for 1 hour is 6 instance-hours, tiny next to minutes of 1.8 s latency. You can also shorten boot lag with lean images, pre-baked machine images, or a warm pool of stopped instances.
steps.idea: Autoscaling trades a little idle cost for resilience; tune the target, the minimum and the lag to your traffic.
steps.caption: Three policies, one fleet.

quiz.q: Six instances are overloaded and CPU reads 100% against a 60% target. Target tracking asks for 10 instances, but 12 are needed. Why is the estimate low?
options: The cloud API caps launches at 4 instances
CPU saturates at 100%, so it hides how far demand exceeds capacity
The load balancer double counts traffic
quiz.why: A saturated metric cannot show the true overload. The scaler under-adds, measures again, and adds more in a second round.

quiz.q: Traffic jumps every weekday at 11:45 and new instances need about 4 minutes to boot and warm up. What fixes the latency spike best?
options: Lower the CPU target from 60% to 50%
A scheduled action that raises the minimum before 11:45
Scaling on memory instead of CPU
quiz.why: Reactive scaling always arrives after the spike. A predictable event is best handled by adding capacity ahead of time.

quiz.q: Why do most autoscalers scale in more slowly and cautiously than they scale out?
options: Terminated instances are billed at a premium, so removing them quickly is expensive
Cloud providers rate-limit termination calls much more strictly than launches
Idle instances cost almost nothing, so there is little reason to hurry removal
Removing capacity too early risks overload and flapping, and re-adding it pays boot lag
quiz.why: Being a little over-provisioned costs money; being under-provisioned costs availability. The asymmetry justifies a cooldown on scale-in.

quiz.q: A worker fleet processes jobs from a queue. Which scaling signal is most direct?
options: Queue depth per worker (backlog divided by worker count)
Total queue depth, ignoring worker count
p95 latency of the web tier
quiz.why: Backlog per worker measures unfinished work directly and responds to added workers. CPU can look fine while the queue grows if workers wait on I/O.

cheatsheet.def: Adds or removes instances when a live metric crosses a threshold or drifts from a target. Handles surprises but always lags.
Changes capacity at set times for known patterns, such as a daily peak. No lag, but goes stale when the pattern shifts.
Forecasts load from history and launches capacity ahead of demand. Good for recurring rhythms, blind to surprises.
Keep a metric near a value (say CPU 60%). Desired count is roughly current count × measured ÷ target, rounded up.
Delay from load change to usable capacity: metric aggregation, decision time, instance boot, and warm-up. Often 3 to 5 minutes.
Period when a new instance is not yet at full speed (cold caches, fresh connections). Ignore its metrics until it is warm, and ramp traffic to it gradually.
Minimum wait after a scaling action before another. Longer for scale-in to prevent flapping.
Minimum survives the first seconds of a spike, maximum caps cost and runaway bugs, headroom (a target well below 100%) buys time while scaling.
